description: Native-environment merge semantics — the shared core behind Node's `mergeIntoProcessEnv`, Go's `MergeIntoEnv`, Python's `populate_environ` and the Java Spring Boot starter's EnvPit PropertySource (bd:envpit-yvyr + bd:envpit-durd). Given a `snapshot` (`values` + `secretKeys`, exactly as unwrapped by resolve-body.json), an `existing` map standing in for the process environment, and `options`, the merge produces three SORTED, values-free key-name lists: `merged`, `skippedExisting`, `skippedSecrets`. Ground truth: sdks/node/src/process-env-merge.ts (`mergeSnapshotIntoEnv`).

notes.checkOrder: Per key, in this exact order: (1) a `null` value is absent — never written, never counted in ANY list; (2) a key in `secretKeys` is skipped unless `includeSecrets` is true; (3) a key already present in `existing` is skipped unless `override` is true; (4) otherwise it is written. Order matters and is asserted: the secret check runs BEFORE the existing-key check, so a secret is reported as `skippedSecrets` — not `skippedExisting` — even when the target already holds that name, and `override: true` never smuggles a secret past the secret check.
notes.defaults: `includeSecrets` defaults to FALSE and `override` defaults to FALSE. The zero-option call is therefore the safe one: it merges only non-secret keys and never clobbers anything the host process already set. This inverts the pre-durd Node API, where the merge could not distinguish secrets at all and demanded a mandatory `acknowledgeSecretsMayBeIncluded: true` acknowledgment from every caller.
notes.includeSecretsIsTheAcknowledgment: `includeSecrets: true` writes decrypted secret values into the process environment, which is inherited by every child process, serialized whole by many APM/crash reporters, and readable at /proc/<pid>/environ on Linux. Naming it at the call site IS the acknowledgment — there is no second flag.
notes.listsNeverCarryValues: All three lists are key NAMES only, so the whole result is safe to log verbatim — same construction rule as ChangeEvent.changedKeys in snapshot-diff.json.
notes.languageLocalOptions: Go's `WithOnly`/`WithExclude` and Python's `only=`/`exclude=` have no Node/Java equivalent and are therefore NOT covered here; each language tests those in its own suite. Every case below uses only options all four languages expose.

cases.name: an-existing-empty-string-still-counts-as-present
cases.why: Presence, not truthiness. An empty env var was deliberately set by someone and EnvPit does not second-guess it.

cases.name: secret-check-precedes-existing-check
cases.why: The key is reported under the reason that actually governs it. Reporting it as skippedExisting would tell the caller 'set this yourself and EnvPit will stop skipping it' — the opposite of what happens.

cases.name: null-value-is-never-written-and-never-counted
cases.why: A null is EnvPit's key-exists-but-has-no-value-here representation, identical to the getters' null-equals-absent rule. It must never become the literal string "null" in the environment.

cases.name: null-secret-value-is-absent-not-a-skipped-secret
cases.why: The null check comes first, so there was no value to withhold. Counting it would inflate skippedSecrets with keys that carry nothing.

cases.name: null-value-does-not-clear-an-existing-env-var
cases.why: `override` chooses whose value wins, not whether EnvPit may unset. A null is not a deletion instruction.

cases.name: a-secret-key-name-absent-from-values-excludes-nothing
cases.why: Pairs with resolve-body.json's `secret-key-absent-from-values-is-tolerated` — the merge iterates `values`, so an unmatched name is inert rather than an error.
